investment_summary:
Adobe's fiscal 2025 showed durable momentum: revenue rose 10.5% to $23.77 billion, operating income reached $8.71 billion, and free cash flow hit $9.85 billion [1]. Total ARR grew 11.5% to $25.20 billion [1]. Consensus expects fiscal 2026 revenue of $26.61 billion (+11.9%) and EPS of $24.47, both dated after the 10-K [3].

At $232.83, the reverse DCF implies roughly zero revenue growth for ten years at an 11.8% WACC [2][3]. That is well below consensus growth of 11.9% for fiscal 2026 and the 10.5% three-year historical CAGR [1][3]. The current price therefore requires growth to fade sharply, or the market to price in AI-disruption risk. If consensus holds, the implied IRR is 17.1% and the forward P/E is 9.5x [3].

The main risks are AI-native competition, rising hosting and inference costs (subscription cost of revenue rose 13%), and thin liquidity after $11.28 billion of buybacks, with working capital of $(37) million [1]. We see the shares as undervalued if ARR growth holds near 11%. The thesis fails if it falls below 10%.
key_takeaways: ARR growth should keep consensus revenue expansion on track, since Total ARR rose 11.5% to $25.20 billion [1][3].
Profitability should hold despite AI costs: operating income of $8.71 billion and free cash flow of $9.85 billion, though subscription costs rose 13% [1].
The shares look undervalued if consensus holds: forward P/E is 9.5x and the implied IRR is 17.1% [2][3].
Aggressive buybacks leave working capital negative at $(37) million, so a growth miss would tighten funding quickly [1].
business_overview:
Adobe Inc. (ADBE) is a software company that sells creative, productivity and customer-experience platforms, including Acrobat, Creative Cloud, Firefly, Adobe Experience Platform and GenStudio [1]. In fiscal 2025, which ended on 28 November 2025, revenue rose 10.5% to $23.77 billion and subscriptions made up 96% of the total [1]. Digital Media generated $17.65 billion, or 74% of revenue, and Digital Experience generated $5.86 billion, or 25% [1]. Total Adobe ARR reached $25.20 billion, up 11.5%, which gives recurring revenue high visibility [1].

The product set spans professional creative tools and enterprise marketing software. Digital Media includes Photoshop, Illustrator, Premiere Pro, After Effects, Acrobat, Adobe Express and Firefly, while Digital Experience includes Experience Platform, Journey Optimizer, Marketo Engage and GenStudio [1]. The main differentiator the filing cites is Firefly, trained on licensed and public-domain content, with intellectual property indemnification for eligible enterprise workflows [1]. Subscription revenue grew 12% in Digital Media to $17.39 billion and 11% in Digital Experience to $5.41 billion [1]. The fastest customer group was Business Professionals & Consumers, whose subscription revenue rose 15% to $6.50 billion on Acrobat [1].

Management is reshaping the portfolio. Acrobat Studio launched in August 2025, and Adobe agreed to buy Semrush for about $1.9 billion in cash, with closing expected in the first half of fiscal 2026 [1]. From the first quarter of fiscal 2026 the three segments will merge into one reportable segment [1]. Capital returns were heavy, with $11.28 billion of buybacks in fiscal 2025 and $2.0 billion of senior notes issued in January 2025 [1]. The shares closed at $304.44 on the filing date, inside a 52-week range of $302.47 to $465.70 [2]. A later consensus target of $266.91 (range $140 to $373) was set after the 10-K [3].
market_position:
Adobe sells mainly to the Americas, which generated 59% of fiscal 2025 revenue ($14.12 billion, up 10%). EMEA contributed 27% ($6.29 billion, up 13%), and APAC 14% ($3.36 billion, up 10%) [1]. The filing does not disclose market share, so Adobe's position has to be judged from its scale and customer base. Creative and Marketing professionals generated $16.30 billion of subscription revenue, up 11%, and Business Professionals and Consumers generated $6.50 billion, up 15% [1]. The filing does not name major customers or state customer concentration, so no single customer dependence is disclosed [1].

Adobe's position rests on the breadth of its installed base. Creative Cloud Pro and flagship apps drove Digital Media growth, while Acrobat drove the fastest-growing business and consumer line [1]. Total ARR of $25.20 billion, up 11.5%, shows the installed base is still expanding [1]. Generative AI is the main repositioning: Firefly models trained on licensed content, plus partner models, let Adobe sell AI inside existing workflows [1]. Management is also consolidating the portfolio. The Semrush purchase adds marketing search tools, and the three segments will merge into one reportable segment from fiscal 2026 [1].

Adobe is an established incumbent rather than a challenger, a scaled platform leader in creative and document software. Its threats are AI-first entrants and cloud-native companies, and the filing notes limited barriers to entry [1]. Market capitalisation was about $125.6 billion at the filing date, on a closing price of $304.44 inside a 52-week range of $302.47 to $465.70 [2]. The consensus rating is Hold, with a target of $266.91 set after the filing [3]. Within the peer group, Adobe had the highest EBITDA margin in fiscal 2025 [4].
operating_results:
Fiscal 2025 was a strong year for Adobe's profit line. Revenue rose 10.5% to $23.77 billion, and subscriptions made up 96% of the total [1]. Digital Media added $1.79 billion to reach $17.65 billion, while Digital Experience grew 9% to $5.86 billion [1]. Publishing and Advertising fell 7% to $256 million, the only segment that shrank [1]. Gross margin widened to 89.3% from 89.0%. Operating income was $8.71 billion, about 36.6% of revenue [1]. Net income rose 28% to $7.13 billion, and diluted EPS rose 35% to $16.70 [1]. Both growth rates are flattered by fiscal 2024, which included a $1.00 billion Figma termination fee that was not tax-deductible [1]. Excluding that fee, operating expenses rose about 10%, which is the more useful run-rate [1].

Cost growth was uneven. Sales and marketing rose 13% to $6.49 billion, mainly on advertising, and research and development rose 9% to $4.29 billion, mainly on compensation [1]. Subscription cost of revenue rose 13% to $2.03 billion, with hosting and data-centre costs contributing 8 points as AI inference became a larger cost [1]. The effective tax rate fell to 18% from 20%, while interest expense rose to $263 million from $169 million [1]. Cash generation improved: operating cash flow rose 25% to $10.03 billion, and free cash flow reached $9.85 billion after $179 million of capital expenditure [1]. Buybacks of $11.28 billion exceeded free cash flow by about $1.4 billion, and $1.5 billion of debt was repaid [1].

The trend against consensus is supportive. Fiscal 2026 revenue is expected at $26.61 billion, up 11.9%, with EPS of $24.47 [3], dated after the 10-K. EPS beat estimates in each of the last four reported quarters, by between 0.7% and 3.2% [3]. Adobe's 41.3% EBITDA margin led its peer group in fiscal 2025 [4]. Net cash moved from -$53 million at fiscal year-end to -$1.12 billion in the latest quarter, so the capital return is now being funded partly from the balance sheet [2]. Future margin progress therefore depends on AI costs rising more slowly than subscription revenue.
risk_assessment:
The most important risk is competition in AI. The filing describes the markets as rapidly evolving and intensely competitive. It names AI or cloud-native companies among competitors, and it cites limited barriers to entry and short product life cycles that could pressure pricing and gross margins [1]. The filing also says there can be no assurance that new AI solutions will be successful or monetizable [1]. The margin exposure is already visible, since AI inference and hosting pushed subscription cost of revenue up 13% [1].

The second risk is cybersecurity. Adobe's products are built into the supply chains of many companies, so one compromise could affect a large part of the customer base at once [1]. The filing says some incidents have already produced unauthorised access to sensitive data, and that controls do not provide full effective protection [1]. The cost categories include remediation, litigation, fines and lost customers, and the filing says insurance may not be sufficient to cover all liability [1].

The third risk is regulatory and litigation exposure, which is the broadest. The filing lists AI regulation at the US federal and state levels, the EU AI Act with phases through 2030, the EU Digital Services Act and GDPR, and describes laws as inconsistent across jurisdictions [1]. Approximately half of employees are outside the United States [1]. Liquidity is a partial cushion, with a $1.5 billion undrawn revolver and no commercial paper outstanding [1]. Funding is tighter than it looks, though. Working capital was $(37) million, the current ratio was 1.0x, and tangible book value was -$1.73 billion after buybacks [1]. Latest-quarter cash of $5.64 billion sat below total debt of $6.76 billion, and the current ratio fell to 0.8x [2]. The Semrush cash outlay of about $1.9 billion will reduce that buffer further [1]. Financial quality scores are reassuring, with a Piotroski score of 7 of 9, an Altman Z-score of 7.01, and a Beneish M-score of -2.85 that shows no manipulation warning [2].
competitors_analysis:
Autodesk (ADSK) is the closest peer by business model, a subscription software company selling design and creative tools to professionals [4]. Salesforce (CRM) overlaps with Adobe's Digital Experience segment in enterprise customer-experience software, and it is the largest of the peers, with fiscal 2025 revenue of $37.9 billion against Adobe's $23.8 billion [4]. Intuit (INTU) is a similar-scale, mostly subscription software company selling to professionals and consumers, with revenue of $18.8 billion [4]. Figma was excluded despite the closest product overlap, because its revenue is only about 0.1x Adobe's.

Adobe leads the group on profitability. Its fiscal 2025 EBITDA margin of 41.3% compares with 31.3% at Intuit, 29.4% at Salesforce and 25.3% at Autodesk [4]. Its ROIC of 41.4% compares with 22.4% at Autodesk, 15.8% at Intuit and 9.2% at Salesforce [4]. Gross margin of 89.3% was second only to Autodesk's 90.6%, and well above Intuit's 79.6% and Salesforce's 77.2% [4]. Revenue growth of 10.5% was below Intuit's 15.6% and Autodesk's 11.5%, and above Salesforce's 8.7% [4]. Adobe's growth is slower than the fastest peers, but its base is much larger than Autodesk's or Intuit's [4].

On valuation, Adobe's EV/EBITDA of 13.59 was the lowest of the four, against 43.63 at Autodesk, 37.85 at Intuit and 29.73 at Salesforce [4]. The multiple fell from 28.4 in fiscal 2024 while EBITDA rose 23%, which points to a lower valuation rather than weaker operations [4]. The data does not state the measurement date, so the comparison is directional [4]. The Salesforce fiscal 2023 figures are anomalous and were not relied on [4]. Adobe's ROIC rose from 28.8% to 41.4% in one year, which needs checking against the invested capital base [4]. Adobe's FCF conversion of 1.38 was in line with peers but not a leader [4]. The data supports the view that Adobe's fundamentals justify at least a peer-median multiple, but it cannot confirm that the current multiple is wrong [4].

investment_theses.thesis: ARR growth stays near 11%, so consensus fiscal 2026 revenue growth of 11.9% is achievable.
investment_theses.evidence: Total ARR rose 11.5% to $25.20 billion in fiscal 2025 [1]; consensus expects fiscal 2026 revenue of $26.61 billion, up 11.9% [3].
investment_theses.signpost: Total ARR growth at or above 11% in each fiscal 2026 quarterly report.
investment_theses.invalidation: Total ARR growth below 10% in any fiscal 2026 quarter, or a cut to fiscal 2026 revenue consensus.

investment_theses.thesis: Margins hold as AI hosting and inference costs grow, because pricing and mix offset the cost increase.
investment_theses.evidence: Operating income of $8.71 billion and gross margin of 89.3% in fiscal 2025 [1]; subscription cost of revenue still rose 13% to $2.03 billion [1].
investment_theses.signpost: Gross margin at or above 89% in each fiscal 2026 quarterly report.
investment_theses.invalidation: Gross margin below 88%, or subscription cost growth above revenue growth for two consecutive quarters.

investment_theses.thesis: The shares are undervalued because the current price implies far less growth than consensus expects.
investment_theses.evidence: The reverse DCF implies about zero revenue growth for ten years at $91.8 billion enterprise value [2][3]; forward P/E is 9.5x and the implied IRR is 17.1% [3].
investment_theses.signpost: EPS consensus for fiscal 2026 holds at or above $24.47, with another quarterly EPS beat in the next reported quarter.
investment_theses.invalidation: EPS consensus for fiscal 2026 is cut by more than 3%, or the company misses EPS estimates.

investment_theses.thesis: Funding is adequate despite buybacks, because free cash flow covers most of the capital return and debt is manageable.
investment_theses.evidence: Free cash flow was $9.85 billion, against $11.28 billion of buybacks [1]; net cash fell to -$1.12 billion in the latest quarter and the current ratio to 0.8x [2].
investment_theses.signpost: Operating cash flow of at least $10 billion for fiscal 2026, with the current ratio at or above 1.0x by the fiscal 2026 year-end.
investment_theses.invalidation: Net debt rises further after the Semrush closing, and free cash flow falls below buybacks for a full fiscal year.
